new_statements.locator: §4.1 Stress, p. 54 (PDF page 9, left half, of; page 30 left half of); supporting statements p. 42 (§1.3.1: 'stress never occurs before the antepenultimate syllable') and p. 55 (short verb forms, rapid speech) and §4.2 Word Tone p. 55
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (15 pp., 2-up, rotated 90, no text) and rendered PDF page 9 left half; it is printed p. 54, header 'A TENTATIVE PHONOLOGY OF ISIRAWA', section '4.1 Stress'. The page scan reads exactly: 'There are three places in which stress may occur: ultimate, penultimate, or antipenultimate. Even though some words are differentiated by stress only: /'topa/ 'tree roots' akar kayu / /to'pa/ 'bow' anak mai / /'tore/ 'tree type' macam pohon / /to're/ 'name of a river' nama sungai / almost all non-verbal words and all the long form of verbs have penultimate stress. The few words with non-penultimate stress are names of places, kinship words, adopted words, and words that are possible historical compou…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word (1-7 syllables). Stress is lexically placed within a three-syllable right-edge window (final, penult, antepenult; never further left) and a handful of minimal pairs are distinguished by stress alone, but the overwhelming default is penultimate: almost all non-verbs and all long verb forms are penult-stressed, and words of more than three syllables are almost never non-penultimate. The exceptions are place names, kinship terms, loanwords and probable historical compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only mentioned for the short form of the verb, which in clause-final position carries the phonological-phrase or sentence primary stress; 'Its secondary stress pattern is unpredictable' (p. 55). No secondary stress described for other words.
new_statements.exceptions: Minimal pairs /'topa/ 'tree roots' vs /to'pa/ 'bow', /'tore/ 'tree type' vs /to're/ river name; non-penultimate stress in place names, kinship words, adopted (loan) words and possible historical compounds; on some words stress fluctuates between speakers within a vowel cluster (p. 42); stress becomes very weak and almost disappears in rapid speech, and the non-phonemic vowel lengthening that accompanies stress disappears with it (p. 55). Tone is predictable from stress (§4.2: the stressed syllable always has high tone in non-verbs; long verb forms have a high-to-low glide on the stressed syllable).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'The phonological word consists of a segment of one to seven syllables with one primary stress and is bounded by a short pause' (p. 54). Data from citation-form elicitation and limited text material (the authors call the analysis above the syllable preliminary). Clause-final short verb forms take phrase/sentence stress (p. 55).
new_statements.identity_note: Oguri & Erickson 1975 (p. 39) note minor dialect differences between villages east and west of Amsira; their analysis is based primarily on the eastern variety (Glottolog dialect Eastern Isirawa east1857), with fieldwork in a village using both. Language also called Saberi.

tone_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1997. Tone systems in New Guinea. Linguistic Typology 1(3): 347-386. doi:10.1515/lity.1997.1.3.347
tone_statements.quote: There [is a] difference, however, between the pitch movements associated with [the] 'accented' syllable in English stress on the one hand and Isir[awa] (Kwerba stock, northern Irian Jaya; Oguri & Erikson 1975) pitch-[accent] ... on the other. ... In Isirawa and Obo[kuitai] the first syllable of the word will always display a higher pitch th[an the] second in the first example (tópa, sótde), and in the second ex[ample] always a higher pitch on the second syllable ... Isirawa (O[guri] & Erikson 1975), which has the requirement that a contrastive pi[tch-]accent be placed in the last four syllables of the word
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Isirawa is classed as a pitch accent language: the accented syllable is fixed in pitch relative to the rest (tópa 'tree roots' versus topá 'bow') and the contrastive accent must fall within the last four syllables. The entry, from the same Oguri & Erikson source, codes stress with predictable tone within the last three syllables; the article adds the pitch accent label and a four-syllable window.
